newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan seen unlikely to hit deficit target.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan seen unlikely to hit deficit target.

text.p: Pakistan is unlikely to cut its fiscal deficit to four percent of gross domestic product as agreed with the International Monetary Fund despite showing strong economic growth, Crosby Securities said in a report.

The report, received by Reuters on Tuesday, forecast that Pakistan would maintain six percent growth in gross domestic product (GDP) powered by by an estimated cotton crop of 10.5 million bales (375-lb each) in 1996/97 (July-June).
But political pressures faced by the government of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto were hampering her efforts to cut the fiscal deficit down to the targeted level of four percent, it said.
Pakistan's failure to cut the deficit in fiscal 1994/95 to an agreed five percent led to the suspension of the IMF's $1.5 billion extended structural adjustment facility (ESAF).
The suspension of the ESAF precipitated a balance of payments crisis, and in October 1995 Pakistan approached the IMF which agreed to release a $600 million standby loan facility.

"It appears the government may not be able to reduce the fiscal deficit below 5.6 percent of GDP unless the growth stimulus in the real economy, due to the better cotton crop, generates higher tax earnings," the report said.

The IMF has also held up payment of an $80 million tranche of a standby loan worth a total of $600 million, due to have been disbursed in June, pending a review of Pakistan's budget for fiscal 1996/97.

A delegation led by V.A. Jafarey, finance adviser to Bhutto, is expected to meet IMF officials this week in Washington in a bid to convince them to resume the stalled loan and start negotiations on a new ESAF.
"In our view, there are still political hurdles for critical tax enhancement measures which have to be implemented if a reduction in the fiscal deficit is to be sustainable," Crosby said.

Traders and businessmen strongly opposed a general sales tax, to be imposed at the manufacturing stage, announced in the 1996/97 budget in June. As a result, the government was forced to offer concessions to certain influential sectors.

The tax was aimed at generating 25 billion rupees to help fill a budgetary gap of 60 billion rupees and bring the fiscal deficit down to four percent. The rest of the budgetary gap would be filled by 20 billion rupees in bank borrowings and by new taxes.

But the report said that a tax on agriculture income proposed in 1993 to enhance tax earnings had not been imposed "due to hurdles set up by vested interest among the country's influential feudal landlords who comprise the majority of parliamentarians".
"Once again, it appears politically inexpedient for the government to push through the agriculture income tax for fear of alienating its main support base," it said.
Giving reasons for Pakistan's fiscal imbalance, the report said 55 percent of government expenditure was used on public debt servicing and defence.
It said the other 45 percent was barely sufficient to cover recurrent expenditure while capital spending on development projects has been severely curtailed in recent years.
